p:
So, thank you for that question. So, I think, um, you know, I think it's probably, ah, you know, a variety of things, um, you know, including some of the things you just listed off, but there's also, um, you know, people's, uh,

appetite to, uh, take advantage of this benefit also varies depending on personal situations. Um, you know, I think if you, uh, are seeing, um, you know, a particular constituency that, um, ah, seems to be, um, I guess less connected with our outreach efforts, we're happy to, ah, you know, follow up and set up, ah, you know, a pop-up up event in your community, just to make sure that we're, you know, reaching as, as many folks as possible. But, you know, as, as we said, uh, previously, it, you know, we're assessing the program every day. And so, you know, where we can find efficiencies and make sure that we're actually reaching, you know, folks that aren't hearing from us, we're open to all opportunities to do that.
Chair, if I may just ask my second.
You may.

Thank you, Chair. Um, well, first, just welcoming you all to partner with us. We do a lot of town halls and events in our parks. We try to program a lot in the district because that draws people out, and then we can offer them services. So, Jamar, I'm looking at you to help

me get, uh, the, the team to do applications live, um, more often in our district. So my, my second question, I want to echo Council Member Hudson's request for data on, you know, by income band, by age, by employment. You said you don't have employment status but by the demographics that you do have, what the enrollment rates are for eligible New Yorkers. Um, and so my second— my last question is, uh, whether the agency has analyzed how many low-income New Yorkers who received fare evasion summonses from the NYPD, um, or arrests or, or any, anything like that were eligible for Fair Fares but not enrolled. Um, and if this is not something that you have looked at or analysis— that has been completed before? Is this something you can work on with the NYPD, since we know the correlation is high?

Um, yeah, we, you know, HRA doesn't have any information about fare evasion. There is a local law that we do comply with where we get, um, files, I think it's monthly, from the NYPD, um, on, I guess, summonses or something issued for fare evasion, and we will mail Fair Fares information out to those addresses to make sure, um, and raise

awareness about the availability of our program, um, to, to people cited for fare evasion.
Got it but you don't have numbers or can you get back to us? Because if you're getting addresses, then you should have numbers, right?
Uh, yes, we can get back to you.
Okay, great. Uh, thank you so much. Uh, thank you, Chair Hudson.

Thank you. Um, okay, a couple of, uh, questions about the legislation. So for Intro 248, it would require DSS to create a system to automatically enroll individuals in city-created benefits programs using information such as tax and social services enrollment rolls. Intro 1028 also requires the inclusion of a conspicuously communicated opt-out mechanism as part of the notice for this program. DSS shared concerns that it would be inappropriate to enroll clients in benefits they do not wish to receive. Can you provide further information about this concern?

Sure, so, you know we very much value, um, you know, people's right to privacy, um,

and the protecting the confidentiality of information for people, particularly who are applying, uh, for public assistance benefits, um, you know, and so our concerns around, uh, clients' consent to, um, where their information is being used, um, you know, and also the, you know, there are, um, you know, state and federal laws and regulations, um, governing, um, and limiting the use of information collected for specific, uh, public assistance benefits and that prohibit, um, and set boundaries for not sharing that, um, you know, outside of, of the intended purpose.

Okay and does DSS anticipate any cost associated with the bill? Um, uh, the Administration is reviewing the proposals at this time, including, uh, budget considerations, and would, would have to involve
Okay. Um, do you— might you know whether or not the expenses would be fully from the expense budget, or may some be capitally eligible?
Uh, thank you for your question. Again, we are reviewing the proposals.
Okay. Does the Administration support automatic enrollment in Fair Fares and other city-created benefit programs?
Uh, the Administration is reviewing the proposals at this time, and we, uh, you know, remain committed to, uh, partnering with city and state partners, um, to make transit more affordable.
Are there any— that was a good answer, by the way, not a yes nor a no. Um, are there any concerns that the Administration has outside of the privacy concerns you've just outlined?
Um, it would be privacy and also, uh, clients' consent and agency to decide what— what programs to enroll in.
Okay. And, uh, what city records could currently be used to identify individuals who are likely eligible for Fair Fares?

Um, again, you know, there are, there are so many state and federal rules and regulations guarding and safeguarding, um, the privacy of clients' information. Um, looking at the open enrollment aspect, for instance, that's people's, uh, personal income information, um, that I

imagine would be governed, um, by a set of also, you know, kind of rules governing tax records and, um, and financial information.

Okay, and so I— you've sort of addressed already the privacy consent or data sharing issues that would need to be addressed before implementing automatic enrollment. Is there anything else that you feel like we should know?
Um, I mean, I think that mainly covers it, and then obviously we'll continue with our analysis on the, um, operation and budgetary implications.
Okay, and just to be clear, I'm trying to help you help New Yorkers. So hopefully we can all work together.
We’re all on the same page.

Yeah, I know it's, you know, we all want to do the right thing. Bureaucracy often makes it incredibly difficult. Um, but I think with a little chutzpah and imagination and perhaps some investments, we can make it happen. So, um, do you know how many current HRA clients— let me ask this differently. How many current HRA clients does HRA

estimate could be automatically enrolled in Fair Fares? If we're thinking specifically about automatic enrollment, so those— maybe the two-thirds that are using the Fast Track. Or I guess you, you, you said earlier you don't necessarily know whether all of the eligible New Yorkers are in your system. Correct?
Correct. Yeah, so that, that would be—
I guess I'm trying— I'm, I'm inadvertently helping you avoid answering my question.
We can, uh, look into that further.
Fair. Um, okay, Intro 825 for replacement transit benefit cards. What is HRA's current policy for replacing lost, stolen, damaged, or destroyed Fair Fares cards?

Um, yes, thank you, Chair, for your question. So currently, um, you know, clients can request and receive a free, uh, replacement card, um, within the 1 year of their enrollment. For subsequent cards, um, you know, they can purchase a new card, or if there's a special circumstance, um,

because understanding that, you know, things happen and people can experience, uh, you know, a lost card, a stolen card, or a damaged card, um, for a variety of reasons, um, we can also accommodate and send out more than one replacement card within the enrollment period at no cost.
One— you- you send out one replacement card, and then after that it's $15, is that correct?
No, we don't charge at all for any replacement cards. So for the first one—
So the first one it's free, and then -
Second one, third one for all, all are no charge. We do not charge.
Okay, so how many times— is there a limit on how many replacement cards one can receive?
Um, you know, by program rules, it is typically one per replacement per enrollment period. But upon—
So one per year?
One per enrollment period.
The enrollment period is for a year? You renew after a year?
Right and then— but if something happens and, um, there's an extenuating circumstance where someone needs a second card,—
Yeah-
Um, we will grant that request and there's no charge to the client.
Okay and then how many Fair Fares replacement cards were requested in each fiscal year '25 and to date in '26? Yeah, you can go ahead.
In fiscal year 2025, we issued almost 95,000, uh, replacement cards. And to date, as of fiscal year 2026, it's almost 60,000.
60, yes.
95,000 is a lot of replacement cards. What are the main reasons?
Lost, stolen.
Lost, stolen. But I mean, people are like literally just losing their cards? 95,000 people are just losing their cards like that?
Yes, yes.
What's it— if they're lost or stolen, you shut that card off before you send them?
Correct. The discount is removed from the card and we send a replacement card and add the discount to the new card.
Okay. Um, how long does it currently take for a participant to receive a replacement card?
Replacement cards are sent via mail, so it takes up to 2 weeks. Uh, generally they get it sooner, but it's up to 2 weeks.
And does HRA anticipate any costs associated with this bill, Intro 825?
Uh, we're still reviewing, uh, the fiscal on this bill.

Okay. Resolution number 52, state legislation expanding 50% fare discounts. Does the Administration support state legislation to expand 50% fare discounts to people with incomes up to 200% of the federal poverty level?
Uh, the Administration is currently reviewing the proposal.

Okay. Resolution number 143, unlimited transfers within 2 hours. Does the Administration support unlimited subway and bus transfers within the 2-hour fare window? I'm almost certain we used to have free transfers.
We'll— yeah, I, I— we'll have to defer to our transportation, uh, policy folks on that, but we can get back to you on our, uh, where the Administration stands.
Okay, but I mean, I'm talking about like back in the day. I, I think we had—
Yeah, but we're speaking as HRAs, so I don't wanna get—

Okay um, 2 hours, this is for 2 hours. Yeah. Um, does MTA have an— Oh, well, this is for MTA. Okay, so, could unlimited transfers be implemented through OMNY without major changes? That's also MTA, okay. Alrighty, uh, any other questions for HRA from my colleagues? Yes, my apologies, Council Member Stevens.

Hi, good afternoon. Um, I'll be very brief, um, because I just want to just

kind of second some of the stuff Council Member Sanchez was saying. Obviously, I'm in the Bronx. We— I'm one of those districts that, uh, has a very, unfortunately low income and I, um, but I know Ride Alliance gave us some information to my office around, like, the low enrollment of Fair, um, Fair Fares and just my question to you is— and forgive me if I missed this— what supports do you guys give folks when they need support around, like, applications and things like that? Because I know, like, specifically in my office, we do a lot of support for folks for all HRA stuff. So, like, people, you got— they have to make copies and all the things. My office, I mean, we used to be next door to you guys, so we've kind of— we— you guys aren't there anymore. We were like there's a default HRA, but now I'm just trying to understand what supports— if I need support on filling out this information and getting this, what, what, what do you guys do around that?

Sure. So, um, you know, we have offices in all 5 boroughs, and we're happy to also partner with, um, you, Council Member Stevens to do a pop-up, um, and have in-person support, um, you know,

at the office, um, at any kind of events or community events to really help support and provide in-person, um, you know, facilitation of the application process.

Yeah, um, 'cause I'm texting to my office right now because we've seen a high number of Spanish speakers coming in our office who need help and support on getting the support. So definitely would love to do a pop-up, but I think that that's something and we have to, like, what does their outreach look like? Are we having it in multi— multi-languages? Um, and then they also are sending them a lot onto some of the CBOs in our community to also support for, like, some of the follow-up stuff that we sometimes just don't have time to do. So, um, and absolutely would love to partner, but I think we also need to be creative about, like, how are doing outreach, you know, in the Bronx specifically. One in five— one in four folks don't even have internet or broadband. So, you know, what does that look like? And anybody who knows who— going to the HRA office is very, it's very difficult and it's not sometimes a friendly place to be. So

just to go there for application, I'm not sure that is the best support where they would go, right? So if I need to just fill this application out, I don't know if I would go there because they're not that nice. So we should really kind of talk about that and what does that look like? And is there other places that they can go to get the support that they need, because my office now is becoming the default. I wanna figure out— we love it, we'll do it, but we also wanna just have additional support. So thank you.

Yes. And our, uh, advertising campaign is multilingual. Um, and also, you know, targeting, um, you know, local and community and ethnic, uh, newspapers and outlets and, uh, social media to really, um, reach the hard-to-reach communities um, in, in, uh, people's languages that are, you know, familiar.

But just like Council Member Sanchez said, um, a lot of folks in our district, you have to be on the ground with them. So they might see an advertisement but don't understand what that looks and how, like, how to go through that process.

So love to do the pop-up, but also we need to think about what are the other strategies so that can be a continuous thing.
Great, we welcome working with you.
Absolutely, Thank you.
Great, thank you so much Council Member Stevens. And Council Member Sanchez has a couple more questions.

Just a quick follow-up. Thank you, Chair. Um, a lot of folks, a lot of folks come to our districts. We help people all the time with the Fair Fares application. It would be really helpful if there was a field that we could mark that said that we help them to do that. Um, and my question is, do you track when, you know, when it's not somebody going to the Fair Fares office but, uh, folks getting external help with the Fair Fares application?

Hmm. Thank you for the question, Council Member. Yes, we have a field at the end of the application that says, where did you receive support? And you can put other and say, your

district, whatever, and, and allow us to know that you are helping your constituents.
So do you have, uh, numbers on how many folks— they're submitting online, but they're receiving help. Do you have that information?
We can get back to you with that information.
Thank you.

Thank you and I- I think that's just, uh, proof that, you know, we're eager to be partners with you all and trying to get our constituents and all New Yorkers, um, enrolled in the Fair Fares program. Okay, um, I believe you all are off the hook for now. Thank you so much for your testimony and for answering all of our questions. We look forward to continuing our work with you. I am going to ask John McCarthy, Dara Goldberg, and Shanifah Rieara to come up. Our general Counsel will administer your oath, and I'm going to kick it over to Chair Abreu. Thank you.

Now, in accordance with the rules of the Council, I will administer the

affirmation to the witnesses from the MTA, please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? John McCarthy, Dara Goldberg, and Shanifah Rieara? Thank you. You may begin when you're ready.

Uh, th-thank you Chairs, for, uh, the invitation to appear. Uh, my name is John McCarthy. I'm the Chief of Policy and External Relations at the MTA. I'm joined by Chief Customer Officer Shanifa Riera to my right and Policy Director Dara Goldberg to my left. We are very glad to be here to talk about Fair Fares. Mass transit is one of the things that makes New York City affordable. Thanks to our vast transit network, New Yorkers pay less for transportation than almost anywhere else in the country. No need to spend thousands of dollars buying, insuring, and maintaining a car. A single tap is all you need to get around New York City. But we know many people still need help paying the fare, and that's where Fair Fares comes in. At $1.50 a ride, participants are paying about 45% less per trip today than they

did a decade ago before Fair Fares started. That's a rare cost in the city that has gotten cheaper over time. Since the program started, we've learned a lot about how participants use the benefits— this benefit. We actually published a policy brief, uh, Dara's team did, with our findings this week. It's available on our website, and I think we've sent it to the team, to the, uh, to the members. Let me run through a few of the headlines real quickly. First, enrollment has steadily grown over the life of the program and ticks up each time the city raises the eligibility threshold. But recently, enrollment growth has slowed as those increases have been more modest. Next, in our report, we found that Fair Fare riders are frequently subway and bus riders, so they're using both modes. Over one-third of customers ride 5 days or more per week, and they're twice as likely than non-Fair Fare riders to hit their weekly fare cap of $17.50. Third, many rely on the subway, and they're more likely to transfer between the subway and bus compared to non-Fair Fare riders. And finally, over

30% of Fair Fare riders' first tap of the day is in Brooklyn, followed closely by Queens and the Bronx. Uh, but Manhattan has the highest Fair Fares usage throughout the day, obviously people coming back from work. We believe more can be done. We know that many low-income New Yorkers earn too much to qualify for Fair Fares today. Even with a minimum wage job, you're maxed out. That's why we support raising the income threshold so that more people can get this benefit. Now, importantly, as decision-makers like yourself weigh the next steps, there are trade-offs between making the cost of transit even lower for the existing eligible population and expanding eligibility to make transit affordable for even more New Yorkers. Broadening access would ensure Fair Fares reaches more people who need it most. We know that Fair Fares can change lives, and we look forward to working closely with you on this important initiative. And before we take some questions, I'll turn it over to Shanifah for an update on our marketing and outreach efforts. Shanifah.

Thanks, John. No question that there are hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers who qualify for Fair Fares but haven't signed up yet. We have been working to close that gap. For a few years now, we have been mobilizing the MTA's own marketing and outreach resources across all 5 boroughs to spread the word and support the city to enroll more customers. Here's just some of the samples of our efforts that we have undertaken so far. As mentioned earlier, self-serve iPad kiosks are now available at our— in our subway system 24/7 at 30 customer service centers in subways, the mobile vans, and at 58 locations, um, we do monthly events and engagements. We also have a kiosk at 3 Stone Street and the Transit Adjudication, uh, Bureau office in downtown Brooklyn, which we also refer to as the TAB office. There, customers can check their eligibility and start the application process. Every month, we host 4 Fair Fares outreach events in our station's customer service centers with HRA at Coney Island, Jackson Heights, Roosevelt Avenue, 125th Street and Lexington Avenue, and 161st Street Yankee Stadium.

Monthly, we hold Transit Talks and Bus Talks where MTA staff shares information about Fair Fares and enroll customers on site. So far, we have completed 40, subway and bus locations. And as of yesterday, we launched a refreshed Fair Fares marketing campaign that is directed to customers to check their eligibility and start the application. You'll see these ads across our 10,000 digital screens in the subway and on buses. Customer service reps will have handouts available for distribution. We'll also give your offices a toolkit so you can help us get the information out to your constituents. We believe there is still room for improvement when it comes to outreach and advertising. And as John had said, we know that there are many working New Yorkers who would stand to benefit from the Fair Fares, um, program. Addressing these needs is a worthy goal, and we stand ready to support the city in raising awareness and keeping New Yorkers informed. And now we're happy to take any questions you may have.

Thank you so much. I would like to thank the MTA for joining us today. Fair

Fares New York City was launched in 2019 and is administered by HRA. The program provides eligible low-income New Yorkers with a 50% discount on subway and eligible bus fares, including the Staten Island Railway, Roosevelt Island Tram, Hudson Rail Link, and Access-A-Ride trips. As of February 2026, there were 379,354 Fair Fares enrollees. Overall, how would the MTA characterize the current state of the Fair Fares program?

Yeah, I'll take— uh, so, look, Fair Fares compared to what we were dealing with before it came into, uh existence, that's a success. Not that long ago, people were paying the full fare, 2019, which I think at the time was $2.75. So we have a 45% discount. Where it's not working is the amount of people who either don't know about it, are not signing up for whatever reason, and just not using this, you know, very important program. Um, the reason we look at this and say if you raise the eligibility, uh, number, you'd have a big impact, is- is because that working person who is, who is at minimum wage is, is, is now above the

eligibility. Think about that. That's a person who would be 10 times a day— that's the person who's looking for this, who's going to your office, going to our offices, signing up for this. They're very motivated. So we're missing that. So the— but, but I, I don't want to lose sight of where we were and where we are today. That's a big— it's a big jump, but there's definitely more could be done.
What are MTA's goals for Fair Fares implementation and enrollment in fiscal year 2026 and fiscal year 2027?

So, um, as Chairman Lieber has mentioned, um, several times, you know, um, Fair evasion— I mean, we tackled and meet about the affordability concerns, um, that our riders face all the time. Um, and when it comes to Fair Fare, I mean, you have heard through the partnerships with, um, HRA, we have really doubled down and amplified, um, our efforts in using the resources within our constraints to get the word out on our own about the program. Again, using— creating our own marketing campaign, um, in addition to the paid ad buys that,

uh, the city runs, supplementing that, um, and- and really making sure that that is well wide and seen, um, across our buses and within our subway cars. Bringing Fair Fares, um, representatives within the system weekly, um, to to do sign-ups at the 3 locations that I mentioned, but arming our customer service agents who are outside of the booth, um, with information about the Fair Fares program and getting them to enroll, but also bringing out members, um, of our team to do, um, these transit talks and bus talks in the system as well as above, um, at high-traffic locations, bringing the Fair Fares team again into the system and having people not only learn about the program, but start the application process or enroll on-site if they see our, um, ads, um, to bring the qualifying materials and documents.

In the MTA's view, and I think you were, uh, John, I think you were getting into this, uh, what are the most significant barriers preventing eligible New Yorkers from enrolling in Fair Fares? You mentioned a lot of folks are— do not know about the program, but can you speak to that?
Yeah, I mean, I'll— you want to go ahead, Dara?

Um, so, you know, we obviously defer to our HRA colleagues who are more closely tied to administering the program and can directly interact with folks who are applying. But when we survey our riders and our customers count by annual survey, and we ask them about their income and their household size, which determines— and so we on our own try to understand people who are eligible but not enrolled. Um, I think, uh, language barrier comes up, uh, frequently, and then not really understanding the income levels and not qualifying, even though some, you know; and we put this in the brief that we shared with you, a, you know, 2-parent household earning the minimum wage with children don't qualify under this program. So we think that the threshold being low is also another barrier. But, um, I think as far as when folks go to enroll and what they're encountering, that's something that HRA would have a closer understanding of.
How many dedicated staff does MTA currently have for Fair Fares Administration?

So, I mean, it will be the entire customer customer team. I mean, that is, um,

my mandate and my mission, um, and really leaning in on our customer service department, which I would say it's about, about 175 people.
And should there be an expansion of Fair Fares? Do you believe that the current capacity you have would be sufficient?
You're talking about the eligibility levels?

I'm talking about if we were to expand eligibility for Fair Fares at the Council level, um, through budget negotiations, I would imagine there would be a lot more folks who would be able to qualify for Fair Fares and I guess I'm trying to figure out if that impacts whether or not MTA would have sufficient staff to administer the Fair Fares.
I mean, so we don't administer the Fair Fares. As you know, it's a city program. We help amplify and advertise and promote and get the word out.

Alright. While HRA primarily manages Fair Fares, the MTA ensures that Fair Fares, OMNY cards, and OMNY Readers provide access to the subway and bus system.

The city provides funding to the MTA for several programs, including Fair Fares, Access-A-Ride, school fares, reduced fares for seniors and disabled riders, and other transit subsidies. How do HRA and MTA coordinate Fair Fares implementation?

So when, um, as mentioned earlier, when we, um, set out to retire the Metro Card, there was a lot of, um, conversation and planning, um, in ensuring that, um, especially Fair Fare customers are very part of that. So they were part of the, um, first constituency group that was part of the pilot in transitioning them, um, over to the OMNY Card, and that level of support have been— remained high, um, as, as expressed in, in previous testimonies.
Is there a formal agreement governing the roles of HRA and MTA?

Um, as far as formal agreement, again, like our, um, you know, focus is about getting the word out. We don't have the ability to do the actual enrollment. Um, we create opportunities for people to start the enrollment process at our kiosk and our customer service centers, but ultimately HRA

is the one that has to verify and complete the process, as well as disseminate the cards.

Fair but Chair, just so you know, we educate even beyond Shanifah's staff in the customer office our frontline employees are educated on, on the program, station agents, others. Um, this is something that, you know, we talk about a lot with our team so that they can reach with the customer and explain to the customer what opportunities are available. So, you know, we'll always look to do more in that area because, you know, we have the people and they're ready to talk more about this and get into the hands of more people.
In the test— I believe in HRA's testimony, they mentioned that there's meetings that happen once a month with the MTA. Do you think that's enough frequency?

I mean, while we have a standing monthly meeting, there is no shortage of other conversation and interaction, especially as we, um, plan and prepare and strategize for these different programmatic events and activities within the systems and in the community.
What data do HRA and the MTA share with each other regarding enrollment and eligibility?

So the enrollment data is maintained entirely by HRA. If we are interested in receiving it, we can, you know, put in a one-off request to get some of the information. Typically, that's shared by zip code. Um, how we track, and in, in some of the research that we put out this week, uh, the program is on the usage side. So we look at the actual transactions and the taps of the Fair Fares cards to understand how riders are using it. So, um, just- just to the point earlier on eligibility and use, even though there are 380,000 enrolled to today, on average, we're only seeing about 60% of those people active each month, so around, you know, 250, 225, uh, unique accounts are tapping with those Fair Fare cards at least once a month.
Thank you for that. How are customer service responsibilities divided when a participant has a problem with enrollment, eligibility, a card, an OMNY account, or a fare charge?
So they can, um, reach out to our customer service, um, um, you know, uh, centers, ah, but then ultimately we work closely with HRA to help remedy and resolve the matter.

Thank you. Now I'm going to transition out to OMNY and Fair Fares OMNY cards. Upon approval, Fair Fare participants may receive a Fair Fares OMNY card through the mail or apply the discount directly to an existing OMNY card, bank card, or mobile wallet. When money is added to a Fair Fares OMNY card, half of the current fare is deducted each time the card is tapped. If a Fair Fares enrollee takes 12 paid trips within a 7-day period with the same card, they automatically receive free rides for the rest of the week. How many Fair Fare participants currently use Fair Fares OMNY Cards?

Um, I would believe that all of them do. The latest I checked in the transition to Tap and Ride is that we're close to 98.5% and the remaining payments are coins on bus where we have not retired that as a payment form. And a very small percentage of employees that still have Metro— like, our employees who still have Metro cards. But I- I

believe— I would have to check that the entire Fair Fares program has transitioned to OMNY cards.
Thanks for answering that question. On average, how long does it take for Fair Fares OMNY cards to be mailed to participants?
That is administered through, um,
Got it. So it is not done through MTA. Is that fair to say?
Alright.
How is MTA assisting Fair Fare participants with the transition from Metro Card to OMNY?

Well, that was— that exercise was done, um, you know, aggressively, um, last fall into the winter as we were sunsetting the Metro Card and switched over to Tap and Ride. Um, and there was a lot of correspondence, lots of customer-facing campaigns, um, and lots of information sent to the, the, the riders, wh— in partnership with HRA to get the word out.
It sounds like it's going well if you have 96%.
Yes.
Yeah.
And it's similar to a senior, uh, half fare card.
Reduced fare.
Yeah, reduced fare. They've also transitioned over to
How many reports of lost, stolen, or damaged Fair Fare OMNY cards has MTA received, and how does MTA handle those reports?

I will have to get back to you on the exact number, but we - when we receive any, um, of those calls, we work with HRA or refer them to HRA, who will start the process, um, in getting and issuing new cards to the riders.
Great. Yeah, if you could just email us that when you can, that'd be great. Has the MTA identified any technical issues with applying Fair Fare discounts through OMNY readers?
None that I'm aware of.
Yeah. How does MTA coordinate its customer service response with HRA when participants experience problems with Fair Fares OMNY cards?

So again, um, whether it's through the, the weekly standing meeting we have, but then also our ongoing daily engagement, um, through our customer service centers, um, if there are calls, there are calls, there's constant dialogue and exchange in an effort to resolve the customer's issues.

Great. I'm now gonna ask a few questions on Access-A-Ride and Fair Fares. Access-A-Ride is an MTA-administered paratransit service for customers with disabilities who are unable to use public buses and subways. Access-A-Ride customers may also enroll in Fair Fares and apply the 50% discount to Access-A-Ride trips. However, Fair Fare participants may only use the discount on one transportation method at a time, although they may request a switch through HRA. How many Access-a-Ride customers are currently enrolled in Fair Fares?
